Title: Causal Forest for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Calculator
Run this analysis with our Causal Forest Calculator. # Causal Forest for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects. Causal forests extend the random forest algorithm to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects, allowing researchers to discover how treatment impacts vary across individuals based on their observed characteristics. Rather than estimating a single average treatment effect, causal forests produce individualized conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates for every observation in the dataset. Standard regression methods can estimate interactions, but they require the analyst to pre-specify which variables moderate the treatment effect. Causal forests learn these interactions automatically from the data using an adaptive splitting procedure that targets treatment effect heterogeneity rather than outcome prediction. This method builds on random forest methodology and connects to the broader survival analysis framework when outcomes involve time-to-event data. * Variable importance scores identify which covariates drive treatment effect heterogeneity. ## When to Use. Use causal forests when you have experimental or quasi-experimental data and want to understand how treatment effects vary across subgroups. The method requires a binary treatment indicator, a continuous or binary outcome, and a matrix of covariates. The causal forest estimates the conditional average treatment effect function \tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x] where Y(1) and Y(0) are potential outcomes under treatment and control. Each tree in the forest splits the covariate space to maximize heterogeneity in treatment effects:. The output includes the average treatment effect (ATE) with standard error, individual CATE predictions, and variable importance scores. When examining variable importance, focus on covariates with high scores as the primary moderators of the treatment effect. By combining the flexibility of random forests with the rigor of causal inference methodology, they enable researchers to move beyond average treatment effects and understand which individuals benefit most from an intervention. A causal forest is an ensemble machine learning method for estimating the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) — the expected treatment effect for individuals with specific covariate profiles. The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is the mean of all individual CATEs. Variable importance from causal forests measures how often and how strongly each covariate is used in tree splits, indicating which variables drive treatment effect heterogeneity.

results.title: Variable importance for causal forests: breaking down the heterogeneity of treatment effects - ADS
results.content:
Title: Variable importance for causal forests: breaking down the heterogeneity of treatment effects - ADS
## ADS. ## Variable importance for causal forests: breaking down the heterogeneity of treatment effects. #### Abstract. Causal random forests provide efficient estimates of heterogeneous treatment effects. However, forest algorithms are also well-known for their black-box nature, and therefore, do not characterize how input variables are involved in treatment effect heterogeneity, which is a strong practical limitation. In this article, we develop a new importance variable algorithm for causal forests, to quantify the impact of each input on the heterogeneity of treatment effects. The proposed approach is inspired from the drop and relearn principle, widely used for regression problems. Importantly, we show how to handle the forest retrain without a confounding variable. If the confounder is not involved in the treatment effect heterogeneity, the local centering step enforces consistency of the importance measure. Otherwise, when a confounder also impacts heterogeneity, we introduce a corrective term in the retrained causal forest to recover consistency. Additionally, experiments on simulated, semi-synthetic, and real data show the good performance of our importance measure, which outperforms competitors on several test cases. Experiments also show that our approach can be efficiently extended to groups of variables, providing key insights in practice. :   10.48550/arXiv.2308.03369.

results.title: Uncertainty quantification for honest regression trees - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Uncertainty quantification for honest regression trees. A new method is developed for quantifying the uncertainties of the estimates and predictions produced by honest random forests. This new method is based on the generalized fiducial methodology, and provides a fiducial density function that measures how likely each single honest tree is the true model. With such a density function, estimates and predictions, as well as their confidence/prediction intervals, can be obtained. The promising empirical properties of the proposed method are demonstrated by numerical comparisons with several state-of-the-art methods, and by applications to a few real data sets. Due to its robustness and accuracy, ensemble learning is a popular method in regression and classification (e.g., Mendes-Moreira et al., 2012). Bayesian ensemble learning (Chipman et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2007) is another approach that takes a weighted average of the trees. In this paper, we apply generalized fiducial inference (Hannig et al., 2016) to construct a probability density function on the set of honest trees in an honest random forests model.
